desc:
A subarray is disjoint if for every two elements at different positions inside it, their bitwise AND is 0 (no bit is set in two elements). A subarray of length 1 is always disjoint.

Return the length of the longest disjoint subarray of nums.

nums = [1, 3, 8, 48, 10]
[3, 8, 48] : 3&8 = 0, 3&48 = 0, 8&48 = 0
result = 3
hints: Checking all pairs inside every subarray is far too slow. What does 'no two elements share a bit' say about the union of their bits?
In a disjoint window, the bitwise OR of all elements equals their XOR and equals their sum. You can keep it as a single mask.
Before adding nums[right], while mask & nums[right] != 0 remove nums[left] from the mask (mask ^= nums[left]) and advance left. Then add the new element to the mask.
editorial: Keep a mask holding the set of bits used by the elements currently in the window. Because the window is disjoint, every bit belongs to exactly one element, so removing an element is just mask ^= element and adding one is mask |= element.

For a new element x, any conflict with some earlier element shows up as mask & x != 0. Shrink from the left until there is no conflict, then include x. Disjointness is hereditary (sub-windows of a disjoint window stay disjoint), so the left pointer only moves forward. Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so the time is O(n) and the space O(1). An element equal to 0 never conflicts with anything.
solution:
def longestDisjointBits(nums):
    mask = 0
    left = 0
    best = 0
    for right, x in enumerate(nums):
        while mask & x:
            mask ^= nums[left]
            left += 1
        mask |= x
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
